\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-barycentre-d12}
\caption{Configuration barycentres on dimensions 1 and 2. Each point is the mean global position of the respondents who hold a complex configuration for the genre named. Only cells with at least 30 respondents are shown, in configurations with at least five such cells, so pre-acquired taste is omitted. Dashed lines mark the centre of the space. The points carry no uncertainty intervals.}
\label{fig:config-barycentre-d12}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-barycentre-d34}
\caption{Configuration barycentres on dimensions 3 and 4, using the same cells as the previous figure. Dashed lines mark the centre of the space. The points carry no uncertainty intervals.}
\label{fig:config-barycentre-d34}
\end{figure}

The cells differ mostly on dimensions 2 and 4. Guilty pleasures sit above zero on volume in all 20 cells, with a mean of 0.87, and justified abstentions sit above zero in 17 of 20 cells, with a mean of 0.29. Taste poses and distant praise sit above zero on status valuation in 16 of 17 and 20 of 20 cells, with means of 1.06 and 1.09. Guilty pleasures, distanced consumption, and justified abstentions sit below zero on status valuation in every plotted cell, with means of $-0.54$, $-0.33$, and $-0.39$. Dimension 1 is less consistent. Taste poses (mean 0.19) and distant praise (0.23) lean toward the highbrow side, while guilty pleasures ($-0.46$) and distanced consumption ($-0.28$) lean toward the popular side. The dimension 3 means lie between $-0.06$ and $0.15$, and we do not interpret them.

Because a cell's position also reflects the other genres its members answer, we counted how many of the other 19 genres each cell's respondents like, listen to, and grant high status, and compared each count with the sample baseline for the same genre. The averages below are means of the cell means, so each cell counts equally. Guilty-pleasure respondents like 9.7 and listen to 6.2 other genres on average, against baselines of 7.9 and 4.4, and both counts are above baseline in every cell. Taste-pose and justified-abstention respondents like more genres than baseline (9.8 and 10.1 against 7.9), while their listening counts are close to baseline (4.2 and 4.1 against 4.4). Distanced-consumption respondents show the reverse pattern, with fewer genres liked (6.5 against 7.9) and more listened to (5.7 against 4.3). Distant-praise respondents like fewer genres (7.1 against 7.9), and their listening counts overlap baseline in 15 of 20 cells. Taste-pose and distant-praise respondents grant high status to more other genres than baseline (7.1 and 6.7 against 3.9), in every cell of both configurations. Guilty-pleasure and justified-abstention respondents grant fewer (3.3 and 3.1), in 17 and 20 cells respectively.

Read at the group level, the counts agree with the positions. Guilty-pleasure cells sit on the high-volume side where their respondents also like and listen to more of the other genres than the sample does. Taste-pose and distant-praise cells sit on the status-valuation side where their respondents grant high status to more of the other genres. The agreement is partly built in. Dimension 2 is computed from the same liking and listening answers, and evaluation accounts for 91\% of the contributions to dimension 4 (Table~\ref{tab:groups}). Across all 20 genres, the individual correlation is 0.84 between dimension 2 and the number of genres liked, and 0.80 between dimension 4 and the number of genres granted high status (Spearman, $N = 2{,}259$). These correlations show how the axes are built, so they do not serve as an independent check on what the axes mean.

These are group averages, not individual measures. Membership in a cell fixes the genre's own contribution, which varies across cells by 0.15 to 0.20 standard deviations on each dimension. Most of the spread between cells comes from the other genres, with standard deviations of 0.37, 0.41, 0.19, and 0.67 on dimensions 1 to 4. A person can hold different configurations in different genres, so cells overlap in respondents. The bootstrap intervals describe sampling variation within each cell but do not account for that overlap or for the number of cells, so counts of cells above baseline are descriptive. Claims about what individual respondents choose need respondent-level analysis of the counts themselves.

\subsection{The Socio-Demographic Correlates of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

We ask \emph{who has complex tastes?} Taste positions are socially stratified, with older people leaning toward highbrow music and younger people toward popular music \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,bennett2009culture-aef}. Are people whose aspects disagree concentrated in particular demographic groups, or spread across them?

We answer this with two aggregate scores. $\Omega_i = \sum_{s=1}^{4} \sum_g \omega_s(i;g)/\mathrm{SD}_s$ sums the genre-based components over the four dimensions, and $\Gamma_i = \sum_{s=1}^{4} \gamma_s(i)/\mathrm{SD}_s$ sums the coherence components. Here $\mathrm{SD}_s$ is the sample standard deviation of dimension $s$'s genre-based component, which is 0.71, 0.74, 0.66, and 1.75 on dimensions 1 to 4. Dividing by these values gives each dimension equal variance, and $\Omega_i + \Gamma_i$ is the sum of standardized aspect-disagreement scores. We chose this weighting after comparing unweighted and eigenvalue-scaled aggregates on their correlations with configuration counts, so the aggregate results are exploratory. The dimension-specific models serve as a robustness check.

Demographics account for $9.9\%$ of the variation in $\Omega$ and $3.9\%$ in $\Gamma$ (Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression}). A model with 24 coefficients would explain about one percent of the variation by chance, so both fits are modest. Across the 48 coefficients in the two models, 11 survive a Holm correction, nine in $\Omega$ and two in $\Gamma$.

For $\Omega$, race and ethnicity are linked to higher genre-based disagreement. Black respondents score $0.62$ higher than White respondents (95\% CI $0.25$ to $0.98$), Hispanic respondents $0.91$ higher ($0.58$ to $1.25$), and respondents who identify with more than one race $1.69$ higher ($0.93$ to $2.46$), and all three survive correction. Relative to respondents aged 18--29, those aged 50--59, 60--69, and 70 or older score $1.09$, $1.56$, and $1.27$ lower, and all three survive correction. The 40--49 coefficient is also negative ($-0.57$), but it does not survive. Some college ($0.57$, 95\% CI $0.27$ to $0.88$) and college-educated parents ($0.50$, $0.23$ to $0.77$) are also linked to higher $\Omega$, and both survive. The upper-class coefficient is $1.50$ (95\% CI $0.66$ to $2.34$), about half a standard deviation of $\Omega$ (SD $2.9$). Gender, household income, and working-class identity show no effects. Postgraduate education, the Midwest, and the South are associated with $\Omega$ only without correction.

The coherence aggregate is more concentrated. Its only corrected effects are for Black respondents ($3.38$, 95\% CI $1.57$ to $5.19$) and upper-class respondents ($10.47$, 95\% CI $6.31$ to $14.62$). The upper-class coefficient is about three-quarters of a standard deviation of $\Gamma$ (SD $13.9$), larger in standardized terms than its $\Omega$ counterpart. Most of the upper-class difference is therefore cross-genre coherence rather than contradiction within particular genres. Hispanic identity ($2.38$) and college-educated parents ($1.75$) are higher on $\Gamma$ only without correction. Section~\ref{sec:coherence} examines the coherence component directly.

The aggregate results depend on two choices. With unweighted sums, $\Omega$ is dominated by Dimension 4, whose genre-based component has the largest variance (3.07, against 0.44 to 0.55 on the other dimensions). Three of the nine $\Omega$ survivors remain. They are Hispanic identity ($0.81$), ages 60--69 ($-0.79$), and the upper class ($1.52$). Black identity, more than one race, some college, college-educated parents, and the 50--59 and 70-or-older coefficients do not survive. Black identity on $\Gamma$ also loses its corrected effect (Holm $p = .23$), while the upper-class effect on $\Gamma$ holds ($12.62$). On a log scale, eight of the nine $\Omega$ survivors remain. The upper-class coefficient does not, falling to $0.13$ (95\% CI $0.02$ to $0.23$, Holm $p = .25$). The upper-class effect on $\Omega$ is therefore sensitive to both choices, while its effect on $\Gamma$ holds in both versions.

The dimension-specific models check where the aggregate effects come from. Because OLS is linear in the outcome, each aggregate coefficient equals the sum of the dimension coefficients divided by that dimension's standard deviation, so the decomposition is exact (Tables~\ref{tab:regression}, \ref{tab:omega-regression}, and \ref{tab:coherence-regression}). The upper-class coefficient on $\Omega$ comes mainly from Dimension 2 ($0.61$ in standardized units, with a corrected dimension-level coefficient) and Dimension 4 ($0.43$, unadjusted only). Race effects come mainly from Dimension 3, which supplies $0.38$ of the Hispanic coefficient of $0.91$ and $0.26$ of the Black coefficient of $0.62$. The age decline on $\Omega$ combines declines on Dimension 1 and Dimension 3 at ages 60--69 ($-1.07$ and $-0.90$), partly offset by positive terms on Dimensions 2 and 4. Of the 96 coefficients in the dimension-level disagreement models, 12 survive correction. On the highbrow--popular dimension, disagreement falls with age from 30--39 through 60--69. On volume, upper-class respondents and those with college-educated parents show more disagreement. On the engagement divide, Black respondents, respondents who identify with more than one race, those aged 60 and older, and Westerners show corrected effects. On status valuation, only the upper class survives, narrowly (Holm $p \approx .04$). In the log-outcome models, the upper-class effects on $W_2$ and $W_4$ persist, while the age coefficients on $W_4$ do not. These are associations in an unweighted online sample, and they do not establish that social position causes disagreement.

\subsection{Which Genres Anchor Complex Tastes? Demographic Concentration}
\label{sec:genre-specificity}

Section~\ref{sec:social} found that demographics account for $9.9\%$ of the variation in the genre-based aggregate $\Omega$. That result does not show where among the twenty genres the patterning sits. We split $\Omega$ by genre. For each genre $g$, we fit an OLS model of $\Omega_g(i) = \sum_{s=1}^{4} \omega_s(i;g)/\mathrm{SD}_s$, the genre's part of the aggregate on the same scale. The models use the covariates of Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression} and the same 2,258 respondents. The genre contributions sum to $\Omega$, and OLS is linear in the outcome, so the twenty coefficients for any covariate sum exactly to its coefficient in the aggregate model. Each genre coefficient is therefore that genre's part of the aggregate association, and the parts can have mixed signs.

Figure~\ref{fig:genre-omega-forest} shows the fourteen covariates with at least one genre coefficient that survives a Holm correction across all 480 genre coefficients. Genres are ordered by their position on Dimension 3 (the engagement divide), running from reggae and rap/hip-hop at the top to heavy metal and indie rock at the bottom. Each genre's position is its mean category coordinate on that dimension across the three aspects. Filled markers indicate corrected coefficients.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-omega-forest}
\caption{Genre-specific aggregate disagreement. Each point is the coefficient from a separate OLS model of $\Omega_g(i)$, the genre's part of the SD-weighted aggregate, on the covariates of Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression} ($N = 2{,}258$). Bars show 95\% confidence intervals. Filled markers indicate Holm-adjusted $p < .05$ across all 480 genre coefficients. Panels show only covariates with at least one corrected coefficient. Omitted covariates are other race, income (\$25--49k, \$50--74k, \$75k+), working, middle, and upper class, and Midwest, South, and West. Upper class is omitted even though its aggregate coefficient survives correction in Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression}, because no genre coefficient does. Genres are ordered by their position on Dimension 3, from the most positive at the top to the most negative at the bottom.}
\label{fig:genre-omega-forest}
\end{figure}

Age is the most widespread pattern. At ages 70 and older, indie rock ($-0.60$, 95\% CI $-0.68$ to $-0.52$) and rap/hip-hop ($-0.58$, $-0.67$ to $-0.49$) account for $93\%$ of the aggregate age coefficient ($-1.27$). The youth-oriented pattern starts earlier for rap/hip-hop ($-0.29$) and indie rock ($-0.23$) at ages 40 to 49. Heavy metal and reggae carry corrected negative coefficients at ages 60 and older, and dance/club does so at ages 50 to 69. Respondents aged 70 and older show higher disagreement in big band ($0.25$), musicals ($0.17$), bluegrass ($0.13$), and gospel ($0.10$), along with several smaller corrected positive coefficients.

Race and ethnicity follow a different pattern. Black respondents' aggregate coefficient ($0.62$) is spread across eleven corrected genre coefficients with mixed signs. Their higher disagreement is largest in rap/hip-hop ($0.36$, 95\% CI $0.29$ to $0.43$) and reggae ($0.32$, $0.24$ to $0.40$), and their lower disagreement is largest in heavy metal ($-0.22$). The Hispanic coefficient ($0.91$) is largely Latin/salsa ($0.52$, $0.46$ to $0.57$). Respondents of more than one race show corrected effects in reggae ($0.43$, $0.26$ to $0.60$), Latin/salsa ($0.25$), and dance/club ($0.22$). Asian respondents score lower in indie rock ($-0.24$) and higher in oldies ($0.14$), but their aggregate coefficient ($0.21$) does not survive correction.

Education and parents' education are linked to a small number of genres. Postgraduate respondents show corrected coefficients in folk ($0.18$), opera ($0.18$), and musicals ($0.10$). Bachelor's-educated respondents show one, in folk ($0.10$), and some-college respondents show one, in jazz ($0.05$). Respondents with college-educated parents show corrected coefficients in opera ($0.08$), musicals ($0.07$), and classical music ($0.04$). Opera and musicals recur across both education measures.

Women show lower disagreement in heavy metal ($-0.14$, 95\% CI $-0.19$ to $-0.10$) and higher disagreement in musicals ($0.06$, $0.04$ to $0.08$). Neither appears in the aggregate, where the gender coefficient is $-0.07$ and uncorrected. Household income, subjective class other than upper class, and census region show no corrected genre coefficient. The upper-class aggregate coefficient ($1.50$) is spread across the genres, and the largest genre coefficient is opera ($0.20$, 95\% CI $0.09$ to $0.30$, Holm $p = .08$).

The genre-level models are exploratory. The twenty outcomes share respondent-level structure, so their errors are correlated, and the Holm correction across 480 coefficients is conservative for that reason. The outcomes are right-skewed, with sample skewness between $0.8$ and $2.5$ across genres, and the intervals rely on normal approximations. The associations come from an unweighted online sample and do not establish that social position causes genre-specific disagreement. Appendix~\ref{app:omega-genres} reports the bivariate Pearson correlations for each dimension and all twenty genres. Those correlations are not adjusted for the other covariates, so they describe dimension-specific patterns and do not replace the models above.

Demographic patterning in disagreement is therefore located in particular genres. Age is linked to the youth-oriented popular genres, race and ethnicity to a small set of genres, and education and parents' education to opera, folk, and musicals. Whether these genres carry the social meaning that the framework assumes is not tested by this design.

\subsection{The Social Patterning of Cross-Genre Coherence}
\label{sec:coherence}

The genre-based aggregate $\Omega$ is socially patterned. Age, race, and education are linked to disagreement in particular genres (Section~\ref{sec:genre-specificity}), and upper-class identity shows no corrected genre-level coefficient. But what about the coherence component---the reinforcing or cancelling of per-genre disagreements across the full repertoire? 

We tested this with the same demographic variables and methods. Demographics explain $3.9\%$ of the variation in the coherence aggregate $\Gamma$, against $9.9\%$ for $\Omega$ (Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-regression}), and only the Black and upper-class coefficients survive correction. The dimension-level coherence models (Table~\ref{tab:coherence-regression}) serve as the robustness check. Of their 96 coefficients, 17 reach $p < .05$ unadjusted and 6 survive correction. The six survivors are Black respondents on $\gamma_3$, ages 40--49 and 50--59 on $\gamma_1$, college-educated parents on $\gamma_2$, and upper-class identity on $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_4$. Gender shows no significant coefficient on any dimension, and household income shows none after correction.

Because $\Omega_i + \Gamma_i$ is the SD-scaled sum of $W_s(i)$, the split in Equation~\ref{eq:genre} carries over to the aggregate coefficients. The upper-class coefficient on the total is $11.97$, the sum of $1.50$ on $\Omega$ and $10.47$ on $\Gamma$, so about 87\% of the upper-class difference is coherence. The same total can arise from one genre held in intense contradiction or from many genres tilted the same way, and social position is associated with which form prevails. This association is descriptive and does not establish that social position causes either form.

Coherence is not always reinforcing. A considerable share of respondents show negative coherence, meaning their per-genre disagreements partially cancel and their total disagreement is smaller than the sum of its genre-level parts. About a third on the highbrow--popular dimension ($33\%$), a quarter on the volume dimension ($25\%$), and more than half on the engagement-divide dimension ($52\%$). One caveat concerns the status-valuation dimension. Evaluation is the only aspect that varies there, so a respondent who grants high status to many genres displaces their evaluation point in the same direction for every genre at once. For such respondents, much of what $\gamma_4$ records is this uniform displacement rather than configural contradiction, which is why $\gamma_4$ correlates with the magnitude of the global position ($r = 0.79$). Where coherence has social structure, then, it reflects these repertoire-wide orientations rather than localized contradiction. The genre-anchored form of complex taste---the kind whose social geography the previous section mapped---is the genre-based component's contribution.

\subsection{Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure. We've traced them from the individual perspective, asking \emph{who} has complex tastes and \emph{what} aspects disagree. But genres are targets too. Which genres attract complex tastes? The answer is that some genres generate much simpler responses than others.\footnote{At the genre level, we measure the proportion of respondents with simple tastes. These are the respondents whose three aspects all agree (either all yes---like, listen, grant status---or all no). The complement is the proportion with complex tastes in that genre (any mismatch across aspects).}

Heavy metal, Latin/salsa, and bluegrass produce largely simple tastes. Respectively, $70\%$, $67\%$, and $65\%$ of respondents respond consistently across all three aspects. You either like them and listen and value them, or you don't. Classical and opera are different. Only $33\%$ and $24\%$ of respondents respond simply to these genres. The rest hold them in contradiction. They might like classical music but rarely listen to it, or they listen out of cultural obligation while withholding judgments about the fans, or they think the music lacks status yet listen regularly. These prestige genres splinter audiences into complex configurations.

To answer this, we need a different analysis. The first MFA treated respondents as the units being analyzed and genres as variables. Now we flip that. Rows become genres and columns become respondent-responses (each respondent's yes/no on liking, listening, and evaluation for each genre). We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This is not simply a rearrangement of the original solution; it is a different analysis that asks new questions. In the original analysis, genres appeared only as variables; we could locate them through the composition of their audiences---the average profile of people who affirm them. But we cannot compute aspect-level agreement from the respondent analysis alone. Specifically, we cannot ask whether genres that are \emph{liked by many} are also \emph{listened to by many}---that is, whether the liking and listening audiences for each genre overlap. We also cannot see whether different aspects place individual genres in different positions. Both questions require treating genres as the units of analysis and respondents as the indicators.

Technically, this flip changes the analysis. Because MFA weights each block inversely to its separate analysis's strength in the first dimension, and transposing reshuffles which variables define the blocks, the balancing weights change. The transposed separate analyses yield different first eigenvalues ($\lambda_1' = 0.153/0.161/0.419$ for preference/consumption/evaluation respondent-indicators, versus the original $0.1550/0.1265/0.1942$ for genre-indicators). The transposed dimensions are thus optimized for spreading genres apart, not respondents. The key statistics we want---RV coefficients comparing aspects at the genre level, and aspect-specific partial points showing where different respondent-groups place each genre---do not exist in the respondent-level fit.\footnote{The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level analysis. Eigenvalues, global and partial points, RV coefficients, and group contributions are numerically consistent.}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map-d12} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA (dimensions 1--2). Black points mark genre compromise positions. Colored points mark aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map-d12}
\end{figure}

From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} more. The RV coefficients jump to $0.92$ (preference and consumption nearly identical), $0.53$ (preference and evaluation), and $0.48$ (consumption and evaluation)---much higher than the individual-level $0.35$, $0.01$, and $0.02$. At the genre level, people who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans high status. Genres that recruit likers recruit listeners too.

This is an aggregation result rather than a contradiction of the individual-level finding. The liking audience and the listening audience overlap for each genre. But the \emph{same individuals} don't always inhabit both groups. The person who likes opera but doesn't listen is in the liking audience; the person who listens but doesn't like is in the listening audience. Separately, they agree. Together, at the aggregate genre level, they agree. But at the individual level, people split apart. Complex tastes aren't something genres do; they're something individuals experience. Which individuals respond simply and which complexly varies person by person.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Genre target profiles showing the percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space has the following eigenvalues ($\lambda_1 = 2.25$, $14.8\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.93$, $12.8\%$; $\lambda_3 = 1.25$, $8.2\%$; $\lambda_4 = 1.12$, $7.4\%$), with the first four dimensions accounting for $43.2\%$ of the total variation. The first two dimensions are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}, and the fourth dimension is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d14}. 

The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($+3.5$), opera ($+3.0$), and musicals ($+2.0$), with distant-praise rates correlating at $\rho = +0.84$ and taste-pose rates at $\rho = +0.59$---against genres most often held in the guilty pleasure ($\rho = -0.79$)\footnote{The correlation coefficients ($\rho$) reported throughout this section are Spearman rank correlations between each genre's position on the transposed dimension and the genre-level prevalence (proportion of respondents, across all 2,259) who hold that genre in each of Ma's eight configuration types. For example, $\rho = +0.84$ for distant praise on Dimension 1 means that genres with high positive values on that dimension tend to have high prevalence of distant-praise configurations, while genres with negative values tend to have low prevalence of that configuration.} and distanced consumption ($-0.82$) configurations. These last include top 40 ($-2.1$), rap/hip-hop ($-1.6$), classic rock/oldies ($-1.6$), and contemporary rock ($-1.4$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement. This dimension, in plain terms, measures the \emph{engagement--detachment} contrast at the genre level. On the positive side sit prestige genres whose audiences are defined partly by abstention from engagement (the listener who values classical music highly but rarely listens), while the negative side includes genres where respondents' disagreement arises from active engagement despite reservations about status (the guilty-pleasure listener who loves the genre but withholds attributing high status to the genre's audience). In effect, this dimension answers the question of whether a genre recruits audiences through engagement or through distant admiration.

The second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}. Genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}; Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}). At the positive pole sit the genres most often held in simple non-taste ($\rho = +0.80$)---rap/hip-hop ($+1.7$), reggae ($+1.5$), Latin/salsa ($+1.4$), and heavy metal ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = -0.81$), as taste poses ($-0.59$), as guilty pleasures ($-0.43$), or as justified abstentions ($-0.40$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($-3.5$), mood/easy listening ($-2.1$), and country ($-1.7$). Opera ($+1.0$) is a partial exception. Its characteristic configuration is distant praise (with $58.9\%$ of respondents holding it in that configuration), yet its position sits on the non-taste side, alongside a low consumption rate ($8.5\%$). The duality is asymmetric in the way complex-taste theory anticipates. The prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is among the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera, against $8.2\%$ for bluegrass).

The partial points reveal how audiences for the same genre diverge by aspect. Like in our original MFA analysis focused on individuals, in the transposed MFA, each genre has three partial points per dimension. One is for the preference-audience (respondents who like it), one for the consumption-audience (respondents who listen), and one for the evaluation-audience (respondents who grant it high status). When these three points cluster together, a genre recruits the same people across all three aspects---likers and listeners and status-granters occupy the same region. When they spread far apart, a genre's audiences are segmented. The people who like it are positioned differently from those who listen to it or who value its fans highly. The configuration axis (Dimension 2 of Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}) shows this segmentation most directly. Rap/hip-hop illustrates the pattern on the simple-non-taste pole. Its liking and listening audiences sit at $+2.8$ and $+1.9$, while its evaluation audience sits at $+0.4$. Classic rock/oldies shows the opposite arrangement, with liking and listening audiences far on the other side ($-4.8$ and $-5.5$) and status-granters near the middle ($-0.2$). Opera splits across the origin, with preference and consumption on the simple-non-taste side ($+2.2$ and $+1.4$) and evaluation on the other side ($-0.7$). In each case, the people who grant a genre high status occupy a different position on this axis from the people who like or listen to it. 

More broadly, three patterns emerge. Opera has the widest spread across its three partial points on the status-without-engagement dimension (3.1 points), where its status-granting audience sits even further toward the prestige pole ($+4.9$) than its liking and listening audiences do ($+2.5$ and $+1.8$). Classic rock/oldies has the widest spread on the configuration axis (5.3 points). Its liking and listening audiences sit at $-4.8$ and $-5.5$, while its status-granting audience sits near the middle ($-0.2$). Most other genres recruit relatively unified audiences where the same people like, listen, and evaluate, or where segmentation concentrates on a single dimension rather than cutting across multiple ways of relating to the music.

The fourth dimension orders genres by the racial composition of their audiences. Blues/R\&B ($+2.7$ and $+2.5$ for its liking and listening partial points), jazz ($+2.4$ and $+1.9$), and rap/hip-hop ($+1.1$ and $+1.8$) sit at the positive pole, and Black respondents make up $19\%$, $16\%$, and $23\%$ of their liking audiences, against $12\%$ of the sample. Gospel and reggae also sit high ($+0.7$ and $+0.5$), with Black shares of $23\%$ and $21\%$. At the negative pole sit heavy metal ($-2.5$ and $-1.7$), country ($-2.0$ and $-3.0$), indie rock, bluegrass, and folk, whose liking audiences are $6$--$9\%$ Black. Across the twenty genres, a genre's position correlates at $r = 0.75$ with the Black share of its liking audience (95\% CI $0.46$ to $0.90$), and dropping any single genre leaves the correlation between $0.73$ and $0.79$. Controlling for each genre's liking rate (the proportion of respondents who like it), the partial correlation is $0.78$ (95\% CI $0.51$ to $0.91$; permutation $p < .001$). The white share shows the mirror pattern (partial $r = -0.63$, 95\% CI $-0.84$ to $-0.25$), but the two shares are related ($r = -0.77$). In a joint model with the liking rate, the Black share is the only one of the two shares that remains significant ($b = 14.8$, SE $4.9$, $p = .008$), and the white share adds nothing once the Black share is included ($b = -0.47$, $p = .87$). The Hispanic share correlates at $0.15$ in raw terms. The female share of liking audiences correlates at $0.39$ in raw terms, but this association does not survive controls (partial $r = 0.37$ given the liking rate, 95\% CI $-0.10$ to $0.70$; partial $r = -0.18$ given the Black share).\footnote{Controlling for each genre's listening rate instead of its liking rate gives a partial correlation of $0.75$ for the Black share (95\% CI $0.44$ to $0.90$; permutation $p < .001$) and $-0.54$ for the white share (95\% CI $-0.80$ to $-0.11$; permutation $p = .014$). Rank-based partial correlations controlling for liking rate are $0.84$ for the Black share and $-0.69$ for the white share. Confidence intervals use the Fisher $z$ transformation with standard error $1/\sqrt{n-4}$, and permutation $p$-values come from 10{,}000 shuffles of the residualized audience shares.} Evaluation contributes only $7\%$ of this axis, and its partial points span roughly $\pm0.6$ against roughly $\pm3$ for liking and listening, so the dimension describes who likes and listens to genres rather than who grants them status. Mood/easy listening also has a positive position but a near-average Black liking audience ($13\%$), so race does not explain its position. Because these are correlations across twenty genres, they describe which genres have racially distinct audiences; they do not show how individual respondents' race relates to their genre positions. Each genre's position is also computed from the liking patterns of the same respondents whose race is tabulated by genre, so part of the correlation with the Black share of liking audiences is built into the construction. A split-sample check, computing the positions on one random half of respondents and correlating them with audience shares from the other half, would address this for the liking audience. We have not run it. The individual-level engagement divide (Dimension 3) is also racially patterned, carrying most of the race coefficients in the aggregate genre-based component (Section~\ref{sec:social}), so the two axes may share a racial basis, although we have not verified that they are the same dimension at the two levels.

Colored points mark aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions). The fourth dimension orders genres by the Black share of their liking audiences, from genres with above-average Black representation (Blues/R\&B, jazz, rap/hip-hop) to genres with below-average representation (country, heavy metal, bluegrass, folk).}

\section{Discussion}

This paper has pursued a geometric approach to measuring complex tastes---the misalignments between preference, consumption, and evaluation in cultural fields. The results support three core findings about musical taste in contemporary America.

\emph{First, the three aspects are empirically independent.} Preference and consumption correlate moderately (RV = 0.35), but evaluation is nearly orthogonal to both (RV = 0.01). This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste concept. If all three were measuring the same underlying thing, we could ignore two of them. But they don't. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable judgments that follow different logics.

\emph{Second, the shared structure spans more than two dimensions.} Dimensions 1 and 2 carry $15.5\%$ of the inertia, and Dimensions 3 and 4 carry another $10.5\%$. Dimension 1 is the classical highbrow--popular hierarchy. Dimension 2 is volume, the number of genres someone likes and listens to. Dimension 3 is the engagement divide, which carries most of the race coefficients in the aggregate genre-based component. Dimension 4 is status valuation, where preference and consumption contribute $4.3\%$ and $4.6\%$ and evaluation carries most of the dimension.

\emph{Third, complex tastes are common in these data.} The disagreement scores ($W_s$) account for $49\%$, $55\%$, $52\%$, and $66\%$ of the average respondent's variation on the four dimensions. Combinatorially, the average respondent holds $10.2$ of $20$ genres in complex configurations. Only 12 respondents (of 2,259) hold no complex configuration at all. Under Ma's classification, almost every respondent holds at least one complex configuration. The classification counts a genre as complex whenever any aspect departs from the others, so part of this prevalence follows from the definition.

Disagreement is only modestly associated with demographics. Where respondents sit on the highbrow--popular hierarchy has long been linked to age, education, and class \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}. Demographics explain $9.9\%$ of the genre-based aggregate and $3.9\%$ of the coherence aggregate. Gender illustrates the point. No coefficient for women reaches significance in the aggregate or dimension-level models in Appendix~\ref{app:regression}. Two genre-level coefficients do, lower disagreement in heavy metal and higher disagreement in musicals (Section~\ref{sec:genre-specificity}), which the aggregate models do not reveal. The dispersion that makes a person's taste complex is only weakly associated with the social positions that sort people by consumption patterns. The genre-based aggregate is associated with more variation than the coherence aggregate, so the weakness of the association applies more to coherence than to the genre-based part. This fits the individual-level theory. The independence of the aspects at the population level generates disagreement at the individual level whenever people don't occupy all three positions simultaneously.

Finally, the duality shows that from the genre perspective the aspects agree. Liking, listening, and evaluation audiences overlap. Across genres, the Black share of liking audiences tracks the fourth transposed dimension (partial $r = 0.78$ controlling for each genre's liking rate). The female share of liking audiences also correlates with that dimension in raw terms ($r = 0.39$), but this association does not survive controlling for the Black share (partial $r = -0.18$), because the two audience shares are themselves correlated ($r = 0.57$). With twenty genres these are descriptive associations, not tests of individual-level effects. But because individuals don't equally participate in all three audiences, complex tastes emerge. A person may be an opera enthusiast (likes, listens, praises), an uninterested person (none of the above), or any combination. The six complex configurations differ in frequency. Justified abstention, guilty pleasure, and distant praise each average more than two genres per respondent, while distanced consumption ($0.4$) and pre-acquired taste ($0.1$) are rare in this sample.

Future work might explore whether these patterns generalize to other cultural fields---visual art, film, fashion---or whether music has distinctive properties. The geometric approach allows measurement of the degree to which cultural judgment is unified or fragmented. The results here suggest that judgment in this field appears more fragmented than a single taste dimension would imply. This rests on one survey and twenty genres.

\subsection{Limitations}

The data come from one 2012 online survey of U.S. adults, and the analysis is unweighted. The results therefore describe this sample rather than the population. Unfamiliarity is coded as non-liking, following the preference measure. A respondent who has never heard of a genre thus counts the same as one who dislikes it, so preference prevalence partly reflects familiarity. Evaluation is a constructed binary, and its coding rule is a judgment call. The 412 respondents (18\% of the 2,259) who are constant within a block enter as supplementary individuals rather than as active respondents, and refitting with them as active yields matched dimensions with correlations of 0.87 to 0.97. The transposed results rest on twenty genres, so the cross-genre correlations have few effective observations, and the transposed positions are computed from the same respondents whose race is tabulated by genre. The regression models are cross-sectional and descriptive, and their outcomes are right-skewed. On the aggregate, the log-scale check of $\Omega$ drops the upper-class effect while keeping the other eight survivors, and $\Gamma$ cannot be log-transformed because 8\% of its values are negative. The aggregate weighting was chosen after comparing alternatives on their correlations with configuration counts, and the unweighted sum gives a different set of survivors, so the aggregate results are exploratory. The geometric measure is interpreted as complex taste rather than validated against an outside criterion. $W_s(i)$ is argued to capture complex taste because a profile whose aspects place a person in different locations cannot be summarized by any single taste position. Its weak overlap with Ma's configuration counts shows that the two measures differ, but it does not show which one better captures complex taste.

\section{Comparison of the Geometric and Discrete Approach}
\label{app:comparison}

\subsection{Comparing the Two Measures}
\label{sec:antinomies}

Geometric complex taste is one way to capture complex tastes, and Ma's categorical complex taste, which uses the configurations, offers another. The two mostly do not coincide. The configuration count correlates only weakly with $W_s(i)$, and the weakness comes mainly from coherence, the cross-genre part of $W_s(i)$. Ma's framework works genre by genre. It classifies a person's preference, engagement, and evaluation of each genre into one of eight configurations. Two of these have the three aspects agreeing, and six have them diverging, such as guilty pleasures, taste poses, and distanced consumption (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines them). Counting how many of a person's 20 genres fall into the six complex configurations gives their total count of complex tastes, the number of genres in which they hold one of these six configurations.

Most of $W_s(i)$ is coherence. It makes up 85--89\% of the variance in $W_s(i)$ on each dimension, and the configuration counts correlate only weakly with it (all $|\rho| \le 0.21$). The genre-based component behaves differently. The total count correlates with it at 0.61, 0.58, 0.63, and 0.24 across the four dimensions, against 0.17, 0.28, 0.18, and $-0.11$ for $W_s(i)$. Most of the disagreement lies in coherence, which correlates with the counts at 0.21 or less in absolute value, because the configurational approach classifies genres one at a time and has no cross-genre term. The total count also correlates with the global positions, at $0.66$ on the volume dimension and $-0.40$ on the highbrow--popular dimension.

Figure~\ref{fig:signatures} shows how each configuration count correlates with four geometric measures on each dimension. The four measures are the global position, the aspect-disagreement score, its genre-based component, and its coherence component. The configuration types differ in their signatures. Distant praise and taste poses correlate positively with the status-valuation global position ($\rho = 0.69$ and $0.42$), guilty pleasures correlate negatively with it ($\rho = -0.40$), and guilty pleasures correlate with the genre-based components on the highbrow--popular and engagement-divide dimensions ($\rho = 0.50$ and $0.47$). These are point estimates from Spearman correlations among $N = 2{,}259$ respondents, with no confidence intervals, so differences of a few hundredths should not be read as meaningful.

Configurations are also heterogeneous internally. Among respondents with guilty pleasures, the status-valuation score $W_4$ has a mean of $4.5$ and an SD of $10.4$, so the same configuration spans different degrees of disagreement, depending on which genres hold it and how much the aspects disagree within them.\footnote{Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} visualizes the full range of within-configuration variation across all eight configurations and four dimensions.}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=.95\linewidth]{fig-signatures} \caption{Geometric signatures of Ma's eight configurations. Heatmap shows Spearman correlations between configuration counts (per respondent, out of 20 genres) and MFA global positions and aspect-disagreement scores ($N = 2{,}259$), across four dimensions and four score types (global positions, aspect-disagreement, its genre-based component, and its coherence component).}
\label{fig:signatures}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Within-Configuration Variation in Disagreement Scores}
\label{app:config-variation}

Respondents classified into the same configuration type show variation in their aspect-disagreement scores across all four dimensions. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} displays the mean and standard deviation of $W_s$ for each configuration, revealing that the overlap in disagreement levels both within and across configuration types suggests why the correlation between the geometric and combinatorial measures is weak. One plausible reason is that the same configuration can span different numbers of genres and different internal structures, so respondents who share a configuration can differ in $W_s$. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} shows the variation but does not decompose it, so this explanation is a hypothesis. The disagreement associated with a particular configuration depends not just on its presence, but on how spread out across the genre space it becomes.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-variation} \caption{Aspect-disagreement scores by configuration type. Bars show the mean $W_s$ for each of Ma's eight configurations on each of the four dimensions; error bars show $\pm 1$ SD. The overlap both within and across configuration types is consistent with the weak correlation between configuration counts and geometric disagreement scores.}
\label{fig:config-variation}
\end{figure}

\section{The Combinatorial Measure and Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation). Two of the eight are simple, namely the simple taste $(+++)$ and the simple non-taste $(---)$, and six are complex.

Under this classification, complex configurations are the common case. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration. The average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$). Respondents often like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't think of as high status. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration. These results describe this survey and this classification, not an established population norm.

\section{Genre-Specific Disagreement Across All Twenty Genres}
\label{app:omega-genres}

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4} show the genre-by-demographic matrices for all twenty genres, one figure per dimension. Each cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable (rows) and the genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$ of the genre named in the column. All thirty demographic indicators are shown. They include the four own-education categories (high school or less, some college, bachelor's, postgraduate), parents' education, the four subjective-class identities (lower, working, middle, upper), gender, the six age groups, the six race and ethnicity categories (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, Multirace, Other), the four income categories, and the four census regions. Each indicator is a 0/1 variable; blue cells are positive, red cells negative, and every value is printed.

The matrices show which genres carry the demographic patterning. On the highbrow--popular dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}) the age gradient appears in the popular block (rap/hip-hop $0.31$, indie rock $0.25$, and dance/club $0.18$ for ages 18--29, against $-0.23$ for rap/hip-hop at ages 70+), the race indicators peak in Latin/salsa (Hispanic respondents $0.44$, White $-0.34$), and Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$) and blues ($0.23$). On the volume dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d2}) the education contrasts appear (postgraduate respondents $0.17$ for opera and $0.15$ for musicals, parents' education $0.15$ for opera and $0.12$ for classical music and musicals) alongside the race contrasts in the diaspora genres (Hispanic respondents $0.34$ for Latin/salsa, Black respondents $0.20$ for gospel and $0.18$ for reggae). On the engagement-divide dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d3}) the first dimension's age and race patterns recur at nearly full strength (rap/hip-hop $0.31$ for ages 18--29; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White). On the status-valuation dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) the associations are weak throughout; the largest is postgraduate respondents in opera ($0.18$).

\section{Genre-Specific Contributions to Configuration Positions}
\label{app:config-own}

Each configuration barycentre in Section~\ref{sec:config-cloud} averages whole respondent profiles, so it includes the contributions of the other genres. This appendix isolates the part of each position that comes from the genre itself. For genre $g$ and configuration $c$, let
$$O_{gcs} = \sum_{h=1}^{3} (z_{c,h} - p_{gh})\,\Delta_{ghs},$$
where $z_{c,h}$ is 1 if the configuration answers yes in aspect $h$ and 0 otherwise, and $p_{gh}$ and $\Delta_{ghs}$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:disagreement}. The term $O_{gcs}$ is the genre's contribution to the global position on dimension $s$ for any respondent who holds $c$ for $g$. Because it depends on the configuration alone, no averaging across respondents is involved. Summing it over the twenty genres gives each respondent's global position exactly, so $\sum_{g} O_{g,c_{ig},s} = F_s(i)$, where $c_{ig}$ is respondent $i$'s configuration for genre $g$.

Figures~\ref{fig:config-own-d12} and \ref{fig:config-own-d34} show these positions for the same 91 cells as the main text. Within a panel, differences between genres come from each genre's standard coordinates and yes rates, not from who holds the configuration. The figures therefore map the genre-by-aspect geometry. They describe a genre's own contribution to a configuration and do not show where the people who hold it sit. Across the 160 genre-configuration cells, the own contributions and the barycentres correlate at 0.84 to 0.95 on each dimension, so the two versions order the cells similarly. The barycentres spread more widely, because the other genres add most of the variation between cells (Section~\ref{sec:config-cloud}).
